market_context: United States/Canada; response to suspected bed bugs with emphasis on confirmation, containment, integrated pest management and professional help.
title: What to Do If You Find Bed Bugs and When to Call a Professional

seo.title: What to Do If You Find Bed Bugs and When to Call for Help
seo.meta_description: Confirm the signs, avoid spreading bed bugs through the home, contain textiles and know when professional inspection is the best next step.
seo.search_intent: Know what to do after finding or suspecting bed bugs, how to reduce spread and when professional help is appropriate.

excerpt: If you find a possible bed bug, do not start spraying products or moving furniture through the house. Save a specimen or take a clear photo, inspect the mattress, box spring and headboard, contain textiles in sealed bags and avoid moving belongings to other rooms. Bed bugs are difficult to control, and a professional experienced in integrated pest management is often the most reliable option once activity is confirmed or repeated.
content_html:
Finding a small insect near the bed can trigger an immediate urge to drag out the mattress, empty the room or spray whatever product is closest. With bed bugs, that rush can make the problem harder by moving insects or eggs into new hiding places.

The first goal is not to make the visible bug disappear. It is to confirm what you found, limit movement through the home and build a plan that reaches the places bed bugs actually hide.

Not every bedroom insect is a bed bug

Adult bed bugs are small, flat and reddish brown. Other clues can include shed skins, dark spotting, rusty marks on bedding and insects tucked into mattress seams or furniture joints.

Bites alone do not confirm an infestation. Many skin reactions look similar. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends looking for physical signs rather than diagnosing bed bugs from bites by themselves.

If you find an insect, place it in a sealed container or take sharp photos for identification.

Inspect where people sleep first

Use a flashlight to check mattress seams and labels, the box spring, headboard, bed frame and nearby cracks. Avoid taking more furniture apart than necessary before you have a plan.

Bed bugs commonly stay near sleeping areas, although an established infestation can spread into nearby furniture and other hiding places.

Do not move the problem into another room

Sleeping on the couch may seem like an easy escape, but it can encourage activity to spread if bed bugs follow the new sleeping location or travel on blankets and clothing.

Avoid carrying loose laundry, bedding, luggage or furniture through the home. Put items that must be moved into sealed bags or containers and clearly separate what is waiting to be processed.

Decluttering helps; relocating clutter does not

Reducing belongings around the bed makes inspection easier and removes hiding places. But moving piles to another room defeats the purpose. Sort, contain and process items in the same area whenever practical.

Vacuuming seams and accessible cracks can be part of an integrated plan, but the vacuum contents should be removed, sealed and disposed of promptly so they do not become a new source of spread.

Textiles need a controlled process

Washable bedding and clothing can be processed using temperature and drying methods that are compatible with the fabric and with an integrated pest-management plan. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) notes that sufficiently hot dryer treatment can be one useful nonchemical measure.

Not every item can tolerate heat. Do not improvise whole-room heat with portable heaters, ovens or equipment not designed for pest treatment. Professional heat systems are monitored to reduce fire and property risk.

Mattress encasements can help with monitoring, but they are not a complete treatment

A bed-bug-rated encasement can simplify inspection and isolate the mattress and box spring. It needs to be durable, fully closed and designed for this purpose.

It does not address insects hiding in the frame, headboard, baseboards or nearby furniture, so it works best as one part of a broader strategy.

Avoid foggers and improvised chemicals

EPA emphasizes that bed bugs are difficult to manage and that pesticides, when used, should be part of a comprehensive strategy. Applying more product or mixing products does not necessarily improve control and can increase risk to people and pets.

Do not use rubbing alcohol, gasoline, kerosene or products that are not labeled for the intended indoor use. Do not apply pesticides to mattresses or sleeping surfaces unless the label specifically allows it.

When to call a professional

If you find multiple insects, see repeated signs in more than one location, continue seeing activity after containment steps, or live in multi-family housing, contact a pest-management company with specific bed-bug experience.

CDC recommends professional help from companies experienced with bed bugs. Ask whether they use integrated pest management and how they verify success after treatment.

In an apartment, notify building management too

Bed bugs can move between units through cracks, utility pathways and moved belongings. Treating only one apartment may not be enough if nearby units are affected.

Follow the reporting process in your lease or building rules so adjacent areas can be inspected when appropriate.

What to do today, in order

Save or photograph the specimen, inspect the bed and nearby area, avoid switching sleeping rooms, contain textiles before moving them and reduce clutter without relocating it. If evidence is clear or repeated, arrange a professional inspection.

With bed bugs, useful speed is not doing everything at once. It is preventing spread while you start a complete, deliberate response.

faq.question: Do bites prove that I have bed bugs?
faq.answer: No. Bites can resemble many other skin reactions. Look for physical evidence such as insects, shed skins, spotting and activity in seams or cracks.

faq.question: Should I sleep in another room?
faq.answer: Usually not as a first response, because moving sleeping locations can encourage spread. Focus on containment while arranging inspection and treatment.

faq.question: Do I have to throw away the mattress?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Many mattresses can remain in place as part of a management plan using appropriate treatment and bed-bug-rated encasements.

faq.question: When should I call a professional?
faq.answer: When activity is confirmed or repeated, appears in multiple areas, is difficult to contain, or occurs in multi-family housing, professional help is a sensible next step.
